paras: The threatened lynching of William Bailey took place at Morris, Illinois, in July 1888, when a sheriff was reported to be having trouble preventing the lynching of Bailey, a Black man accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl. The episode is known only from a single sentence carried in newspaper roundups, and no report of its outcome was found.

According to the item, Bailey, described as "a negro," was accused of having assaulted "a frail thirteen-year-old girl" at Morris. The sheriff was said to be "having trouble" preventing his lynching, which suggests that Bailey was in the sheriff's hands, though the report does not say where he was held. It gives no date for the alleged assault and does not describe who threatened the lynching, how many there were, or what they did.
No report of whether a lynching was attempted, or of a trial of Bailey, was found in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal ran the sentence on July 17, 1888, under "Brief Mention" in its Illinois column, among items from dispatches dated July 16, next to a report of an interracial wedding at Marshall. Eleven days later, the Western Kansas World of WaKeeney reprinted the same wording in a "Domestic" roundup, adding "Illinois" after Morris and printing the name as "William Cailey." Both versions stated the assault as fact rather than as a charge and offered no comment on the threatened mob.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Bailey
bases: Both items report that a sheriff at Morris was having trouble preventing the lynching of a Black man accused of assaulting a girl, a threatened lynching with no killing reported (A1, A2).

The items describe a threatened lynching that a sheriff was trying to prevent; no killing is reported and no follow-up was found (A1, A2). The threat was extralegal and rested on an accusation of assault, but the size of the crowd is not given.
The two items are word-for-word versions of one news paragraph, the later in a Kansas roundup, so they are not independent reports (A1, A2).
